v1.1.1 — less load on the nodes that serve the network, a rich list, and the silvra.net look

No reset, no coordinated update: replace the binary and restart; data, key and stake stay. This
release changes nothing a block contains or how it is executed. Protocol 2 activates at block
750000 as voted; 1.1.0 and 1.1.1 both run it. **A node still on 1.0.x stops at block 750000** and
goes on as soon as it runs 1.1.0 or this release.

**Why update: the network leans on whoever serves it**

On 2026-10-18 ten validators dropped out together and the chain slowed to 5–6 s a block for most
of three hours; on 2026-10-20 the production validator, on a home line, fell behind and was jailed.
Both times the line that serves the network was full — not with blocks the chain needed, but with
catch-up traffic nobody needed:

- **A node pulls blocks over RPC only as a last resort.** Every node asked its sync peer
  (`node.silvra.net` by default) for blocks whenever it was one to three blocks behind, every four
  seconds — and those blocks were already on their way over P2P. A validator now pulls only when
  the gap has stopped closing for 30 seconds, and backs off when a pull fails (8 s, doubling up to
  2 minutes). A node outside the validator set (a follower, a wallet's node, an explorer) that was
  level with its peer a moment ago still pulls on the next poll, because P2P no longer brings it
  finished blocks. A node held after a failed startup sync pulls at once, as before.
- **A node asks for a batch it can receive.** A node that paces its block batches
  (`HELIX_RPC_SYNC_RATE`) now refuses one its client cannot receive within the client's 30 s,
  before sending a byte, and says how many blocks would fit (`x-helix-sync-fits`); this release
  asks for that many. Until now such a batch was sent until the client gave up, then sent again —
  about half of what the production node uploaded for syncing was thrown away like this.
- **A missed block is served again only to a peer that is stuck.** A node that heard a peer
  announce a tip below its own sent it the blocks it seemed to lack — to every peer, with a full
  certificate. Announcements are up to 30 seconds old, so on a network of fifty nodes almost every
  peer looked behind for a moment: the production node re-published 52 of 57 finished blocks in two
  minutes. It now serves only a peer whose announced tip has not moved since its last announcement.

Measured on the production node after deploying these: upload from about 770 to about 200 kB/s,
block re-publishing from about one a second to none. The first point helps the network only once
the nodes that pull — yours — run this release.

**A rich list**

`GET /accounts/top?limit=N` (default 25, at most 100): the accounts holding the most, each with its
liquid balance, own stake, delegations at today's value and unbonding stake, plus the same four
summed over every account. The explorer draws it on its new **Network** page, next to charts of the
block interval, transactions per block and the base fee, and how many validators it takes to stop
or to control the chain.

**The silvra.net look**

The desktop wallet and the node's own status page now look like the website and the explorer: the
round camouflage logo (also the wallet's app icon), night olive with amber, the site's type —
served by the node itself, so the status page still loads nothing from anyone else. The status page
also no longer says a validator "holds no stake" when it is jailed, and no longer hides the disk,
memory and load readings behind a long sync checkpoint.
